episodes.title: Chandrayaan-2's Orbiter, Still at Work
sources: ISRO, Chandrayaan-2 mission page (isro.gov.in/Chandrayaan_2.html): 100 km lunar polar orbit; Vikram separated 2 September 2019; eight orbiter instruments; OHRC has the best resolution (0.3 m) of any lunar orbiter camera; expected life of about seven years against a planned one year

Wikipedia, 'Chandrayaan-2' (summary read): launched 22 July 2019 on LVM3-M1; Vikram crashed 6 September 2019 after a software glitch; the orbiter relayed for Chandrayaan-3; CLASS mapped sodium; CHACE-2 detected argon-40; chromium and manganese detected; XSM and CLASS observed a May 2024 solar flare

quiz.q: What did the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter do for Chandrayaan-3?
quiz.why: In 2023 the orbiter relayed communication for the Chandrayaan-3 lander.

quiz.q: Roughly how high above the Moon does the orbiter fly?
quiz.why: ISRO gives a 100 km lunar polar orbit.

quiz.q: Which Chandrayaan-2 instrument is the high-resolution camera?
quiz.why: OHRC, the Orbiter High Resolution Camera, resolves about 0.3 m.

review.note: Facts were read against ISRO's Chandrayaan-2 page; launch date, crash cause and science results come from the Wikipedia article and should be checked against ISRO before approval. The 'Relay' ring is decorative (full ring). Moving facts: the orbiter's remaining life and its science results keep changing.

episodes.title: Ballistic or Cruise: Two Kinds of Missile
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ballistic missile' (summary read): powered only for a short initial period, most of the flight unpowered; boost, mid-course and terminal phases; long-range (ICBM) trajectories peak well above 1,000 km, outside the atmosphere
Wikipedia, 'Cruise missile' (summary read): self-navigating, flies a non-ballistic, often very low path; aerodynamically guided in powered flight and stays within the atmosphere
PIB, 11 March 2024 (PRID 2013549): Mission Divyastra, the first flight test of Agni-5 with Multiple Independently Targetable Re-entry Vehicle technology, from Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island, Odisha
DRDO, BrahMos page: BrahMos is a joint venture of DRDO (India) and NPOM (Russia); inducted into the Indian Navy and Army

quiz.q: For most of its flight, a ballistic missile is…
quiz.why: It burns only briefly at the start, then coasts along a ballistic path.

quiz.q: What did Mission Divyastra (March 2024) test?
options: Agni-5 with multiple independently targetable warheads
quiz.why: PIB: the first flight test of Agni-5 with MIRV technology.

quiz.q: Which statement about cruise missiles is correct?
options: They stay in the atmosphere and are powered through flight
quiz.why: Cruise missiles fly like small planes, powered and within the air.

review.note: Physics of the two types comes from Wikipedia summaries; official confirmation is from PIB (Divyastra) and DRDO (BrahMos). No BrahMos speed is given because the figure was not read from an official page. The archive photo is from the SDASM negative collection; check it reads correctly (not an inverted negative) and that no logo shows. Only one picture was found under an allowed licence, so the video leans on diagrams. Moving facts: missile tests are frequent; check nothing newer changes the India card. The ICBM peak height was softened to 'more than a thousand kilometres', which every source agrees on.

episodes.title: INS Vikrant: A Carrier Built in India
sources: PIB backgrounder, 24 October 2025 (PRID 2182277): commissioned 2 September 2022 at Kochi; 76% indigenous content; 30,000 tonnes of SAIL steel; designed by the Navy's Warship Design Bureau, built by Cochin Shipyard; largest warship built in India; 262.5 m long, 61.6 m wide, about 45,000 tonnes; STOBAR (ski-jump take-off, arrester-wire recovery); up to 30 aircraft including MiG-29K, MiG-29KUB, Kamov-31, MH-60R, Chetak and ALH; named after INS Vikrant (R11), decommissioned 1997; over 550 OEMs and about 100 MSMEs

quiz.q: What share of INS Vikrant is indigenous, according to PIB?
quiz.why: PIB gives 76% indigenous content.

quiz.q: How do aircraft take off from INS Vikrant?
quiz.why: Vikrant uses STOBAR: ski-jump take-off, arrester-wire landing.

quiz.q: Which shipyard built INS Vikrant?
quiz.why: Designed by the Navy's Warship Design Bureau, built by Cochin Shipyard.

review.note: All facts are from one PIB backgrounder (October 2025). No licensed photo of Vikrant itself was found, so the video uses diagrams and a US Navy photo of an Indian Navy MiG-29K; crop to the jet so the US carrier below doesn't read as Vikrant, and check no hull number shows. Moving facts: the air wing mix changes as new aircraft arrive.

episodes.title: Tejas: India's Light Combat Aircraft
sources: PIB (relid 146717): Tejas designed by ADA (DRDO) with HAL as principal partner; first flight of TD1 on 4 January 2001; project from the late 1980s
PIB (relid 146697): Tejas inducted into No. 45 Squadron 'Flying Daggers' on 1 July 2016; the squadron last flew the MiG-21 Bis

PIB, 30 June 2023 (PRID 1936373): named Tejas in 2003; multi-role; inherently unstable design for manoeuvrability; No. 18 Squadron the second (May 2020); Ex-Desert Flag in the UAE in March 2023 was its first exercise abroad; order for 83 LCA Mk-1A

quiz.q: Which agency designed Tejas?
quiz.why: ADA under DRDO designed it, with HAL as principal partner.

quiz.q: When did Tejas first fly?
quiz.why: TD1 flew on 4 January 2001.

quiz.q: Which aircraft had No. 45 Squadron last flown before Tejas?
quiz.why: PIB: the Flying Daggers last flew the MiG-21 Bis.

review.note: Facts were read against three PIB releases. 'Being delivered' for the Mk-1A order is a soft phrase; check the delivery status before approval. Check the two photos for any visible pilot faces; crop if so. Moving facts: Mk-1A deliveries and squadron count.

episodes.title: What 5G Actually Changes
sources: ITU-R Report M.2410-0, minimum requirements for IMT-2020: downlink peak data rate 20 Gbit/s; user-plane latency 4 ms for eMBB and 1 ms for URLLC; connection density 1,000,000 devices per km²
ITU-R Recommendation M.2083: three usage scenarios, eMBB, URLLC and mMTC

PIB (PRID 1863659): 5G launched on 1 October 2022 at India Mobile Congress, Pragati Maidan; 51,236 MHz allocated; DoT 5G test bed with IITs, IISc and SAMEER from 2018; IoT, M2M and edge-computing use cases

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of ITU's three 5G usage scenarios?
quiz.why: The three are eMBB, URLLC and mMTC.

quiz.q: What latency target does ITU set for ultra-reliable 5G links?
quiz.why: 1 ms user-plane latency for URLLC (4 ms for broadband).

quiz.q: When were 5G services launched in India?
quiz.why: PIB: launched on 1 October 2022 at India Mobile Congress.

review.note: Targets come from ITU-R M.2410-0 and M.2083, India facts from PIB. These are design targets, not speeds users see; the script says 'targets'. The 2022 auction year is inferred from the PIB launch release, which gives the spectrum allotted; check. Avoid any brand name on the tower photos. The million-devices ring is decorative (full ring). Moving facts: India's 5G coverage and user numbers (none given).

episodes.title: Quantum Computing, Simply
sources: NIST, 'Quantum computing explained': bits are 0 or 1; qubits can be in superposition; entanglement; qubits are fragile and today's machines are error-prone; many need very cold temperatures; quantum computers would work alongside classical ones on materials, drug discovery and cybersecurity; threat to current encryption and the move to post-quantum cryptography

PIB, 19 April 2023 (PRID 1917888): National Quantum Mission approved at ₹6003.65 crore for 2023-24 to 2030-31; intermediate-scale quantum computers with 50–1000 physical qubits in 8 years; satellite-based secure quantum communication over 2000 km; four thematic hubs

quiz.q: What is superposition?
options: A qubit holding a blend of 0 and 1
Cooling a chip to absolute zero
quiz.why: A qubit can be in a combination of 0 and 1, unlike a bit.

quiz.q: What qubit range does India's National Quantum Mission target within 8 years?
quiz.why: PIB: intermediate-scale computers with 50–1000 physical qubits.

quiz.q: Why do many quantum computers need extreme cold?
options: Qubits are fragile and lose their state to heat and noise
quiz.why: Heat and noise disturb qubits; cold keeps them stable.

review.note: Facts were read against NIST's explainer and PIB's NQM release. The analogy 'like a switch' is a simplification NIST itself uses for bits. Moving facts: qubit counts worldwide change fast; none are quoted.

episodes.title: CRISPR: Editing Genes
sources: MedlinePlus Genetics (US National Library of Medicine), 'What are genome editing and CRISPR-Cas9?': adapted from a bacterial defence; bacteria store virus DNA in CRISPR arrays, make matching RNA, and Cas9 cuts the virus DNA; researchers make a guide RNA plus Cas9 to cut a target, and the cell's repair machinery adds, deletes or replaces DNA; faster, cheaper, more accurate and more efficient than other methods; studied for cystic fibrosis, haemophilia and sickle cell disease; most changes are in somatic cells; germline editing raises ethical concerns
NHGRI, genome editing page: CRISPR is simpler, faster and cheaper than earlier methods

quiz.q: In CRISPR-Cas9, what does Cas9 do?
options: Cuts the DNA at the target
quiz.why: The guide RNA finds the spot; Cas9 cuts; the cell repairs.

quiz.q: Where did the CRISPR idea come from?
quiz.why: It is adapted from how bacteria fight viruses.

quiz.q: Why does germline editing raise ethical concerns?
options: It is slower than somatic editing
Its changes can pass to future generations
quiz.why: Edits to eggs, sperm or embryos are inherited.

review.note: Facts were read against MedlinePlus Genetics and NHGRI. 'Sickle cell is a big concern in parts of India' is general knowledge, not from those sources; cut it or add a source (for example the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission on PIB) before approval. Moving facts: approved CRISPR therapies are changing; none is named.

episodes.title: How a Nuclear Reactor Makes Power
sources: US EIA, 'Nuclear power plants': fission splits uranium atoms, releasing heat and neutrons in a chain reaction; fuel is uranium ceramic pellets stacked in 12-foot fuel rods; heat makes steam that spins turbines driving generators; cooling towers or water from lakes, rivers or the ocean
US EIA, 'Types of reactors': boiling-water and pressurized-water reactors
Wikipedia, 'Control rod' (read): control rods contain neutron absorbers such as boron or cadmium; inserting them controls the chain reaction; fully inserted they shut the reactor down
Wikipedia, 'Pressurized heavy-water reactor' (read): heavy water as coolant and moderator; natural uranium fuel; IPHWR-220 and IPHWR-700 are Indian designs

quiz.q: What do control rods do?
options: Absorb neutrons to slow or stop the chain reaction
quiz.why: They soak up neutrons; fully inserted, they stop the reaction.

quiz.q: What lets India's PHWRs run on natural uranium?
quiz.why: Heavy water is an efficient moderator, so enrichment isn't needed.

quiz.q: In a nuclear power station, what spins the turbine?
quiz.why: Fission heat makes steam; the steam spins the turbine.

review.note: Basics were read against two US EIA pages; control rods and the PHWR come from Wikipedia articles because NRC and NPCIL pages didn't return readable text here. 'Most of India's reactors are PHWRs' is not stated in those sources; check it against NPCIL's plant list before approval. The TVA animation is of a boiling-water reactor, which India doesn't use; it illustrates the steam cycle only. Start times (t) were chosen blind. Moving facts: India's reactor count.

episodes.title: Space Debris: Junk in Orbit
sources: NASA Orbital Debris Program Office, FAQ (orbitaldebris.jsc.nasa.gov/faq): kinds of debris (derelict spacecraft, upper stages, fragments from explosions and collisions, paint flecks); the US Space Surveillance Network had catalogued more than 34,000 objects; routinely tracks objects larger than about 10 cm; debris in low Earth orbit travels at 7–8 km/s; average impact speed about 10 km/s, up to about 15 km/s; Fengyun-1C destruction (2007) and Iridium 33–Cosmos 2251 collision (2009) greatly increased large debris; the ISS manoeuvres when collision risk exceeds 1 in 10,000 (41 times since 1999); debris below 600 km normally falls back within several years

quiz.q: About how fast does debris travel in low Earth orbit?
quiz.why: NASA ODPO: about 7 to 8 km per second.

quiz.q: What size of object does the US network routinely track?
quiz.why: Routine tracking covers objects bigger than about 10 cm.

quiz.q: What happens to debris below about 600 km?
options: It stays for millions of years
It is collected by the ISS
It normally falls back within several years
quiz.why: Air drag pulls low debris down within several years.

review.note: All facts are from the NASA ODPO FAQ. Countries are not named on purpose. Moving facts: the catalogued count (34,000+) and the ISS manoeuvre count rise over time; the count of manoeuvres is left out of the script. No India angle was sourced in time; ISRO's debris-free missions goal could be added with a PIB source.

episodes.title: How a Solar Panel Makes Electricity
sources: US EIA, 'Photovoltaics and electricity': PV cells are made of semiconductor material; photons are reflected, pass through or are absorbed; absorbed energy dislodges electrons, which migrate to the front surface, creating a charge imbalance; conductors collect the current; cells make panels (modules), panels make arrays; PV cells produce direct current, and inverters convert it to alternating current used by the grid

quiz.q: Which sunlight makes electricity in a solar cell?
quiz.why: Only absorbed photons free electrons.

quiz.q: What does an inverter do?
options: Turns the panel to face the Sun
quiz.why: Cells make direct current; inverters convert it to alternating current.

quiz.q: What is a group of solar panels wired together called?
quiz.why: Cells make panels (modules); panels make arrays.

review.note: All facts are from the US EIA photovoltaics page. 'Weather satellites can see them' is drawn from the CIRA/NOAA footage title itself; check the clip shows a solar farm glint before approval. The fan in the opening is an illustration, not a claim. Moving facts: none.
